utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-94-2-PT, the Prosecutor versus Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand? I need someone -- Usher, I need someone to assist the accused and make sure that he can -- he has the interpretation equipment on. Can you -- is it better now? Can you hear what I'm saying in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. I'm Upawansa Yapa, appearing for the Prosecution with Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. William Smith, and Ms. Diane Boles. She's our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you all. Appearances for the Defence, the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Howard Morrison together with Tanja Radosavljevic for the defendant Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you both. So I need hardly point out that this is a Status Conference that is being held pursuant to Rule 65 bis, the last Status Conference having been held on the 7th of November. So we are within the 120-day time limit that is indicated, is imposed by the Rule. I also wish to remind the parties that the purpose of such Status Conference is to ensure an efficient and expeditious preparation for the trial and to give an opportunity to the accused, Mr. Nikolic in this case, to raise any issue that he might like in relation to his state of health, be it physical or mental, or in any case relating to his state of detention in the Detention Unit here in The Hague. I also have been informed -- I am informed by my senior legal counsel that, as planned, he presided over a 65 ter meeting these last few days and that practically all the matters that will be here -- that are on today's agenda were discussed during that meeting, and I am also informed that, as far as certain issues are concerned, we don't need to discuss them at any length here because they have been fully aired and debated during the 65 ter meeting. So the first item that I should like to deal with is the pending motions, and the first of these is the interlocutory appeal, and I am informed that this was thrashed out during the 65 ter meeting and I need not touch upon it here. You are or we are all expecting a decision by the Appeals Chamber very likely towards mid-April or before mid-April. Obviously, the plans that we will make will focus on this date as the most likely date, but if there is a delay, obviously we will have to come back to this matter and the ensuing problems later on. Then there is a very recent motion that this Chamber has received, and that's a depositions motion, this motion having been filed only a few days ago, namely on the 28th of February, 2003, in which the Prosecution is requesting from this Trial Chamber, from this Chamber, an order authorising the taking of depositions from six Prosecution witnesses prior to the commencement of the trial. It seems, at least from the substance of the motion itself, that the idea behind this motion is the age and state of health of these witnesses and, therefore, the idea is to preserve, to ensure that there is a deposition just in case the state of health deteriorates or they die, and also, anyway, to shorten the length of trial by securing depositions being taken even before the trial starts. The procedure that is being suggested by the Prosecution is that the depositions be taken during a three-day period here in The Hague in the presence of the accused, and for this -- for these deposition, for the purposes of these depositions, the Defence, of course, will be able to cross-examine witnesses and depositions will be made available on video and in transcript form. The legal basis that is being provided by the Prosecution as justification for the request is that -- is basically based on Rule 71 and can be found in the motion itself. I take it that the Defence filed their response only a few days ago, on the 3rd of March. There is no objection in principle to the taking of depositions. Defence, however, has to rely on the good faith of the Prosecution in relation to the assessment of the state of health of the witnesses, and the usefulness of these depositions obviously has to be viewed in relation to the trial date, which, to me, this last point is perhaps the most important of all, together with the -- with whether the state of health of these six individuals, six persons, is such as to really present a predicament and justify the concern that you have, Mr. Yapa, representing the Prosecution, that you may not be in a position to make any use of these witnesses later on if we don't take these depositions in a timely fashion before the trial starts. I personally should like you both to address this point -- on these two points, plus another concern that I personally have as a Pre-Trial Judge. In all probability, as I see it, I won't be the Presiding Judge in the trial when this takes place, and I personally feel a little bit awkward in granting the hearing of the evidence of these witnesses by the procedure that is being suggested, in a way depriving the future Presiding Judge in this trial for the opportunity of having them here in open court and testify viva voce. That is the other problem that I have. But having said that, I should like you to address these issues, keeping in mind that, as I will be saying later on, there is a strong probability that the trial may start end of April or early May. Mr. Yapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On this question of our motion for the depositions, as Your Honour was pleased to explain, our main concern was the age and the state of health of the witnesses. We cannot be definite about any of these matters. It is actually as a matter of precaution that we filed the motion. It may be said if there is any kind of predicament to any of the witnesses, it may be said that we were too late in making the application or we need not have made the application because the witnesses are hale and hearty at the time the depositions have to be taken and the trial is to be taken up. So it is only as a matter of precaution and also as an abundance of caution that we filed this motion before Your Honour. So if the trial date is earlier, Your Honours may, or whoever is taking the decision, may consider that it may not be required to have depositions because the trial date is coming close by. But if there is a likelihood of the trial date going down, then I would submit that it will be in the interests of justice to have the statements or have the evidence of these witnesses recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Yapa. That is indeed -- you've been most reasonable, and I thank you for that. Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take the same position as to the dates. Plainly if the trial is going to be in May, that is when the depositions were proposed in any event so obviously there would be no point in doing it in those circumstances. I think the only real issue is whether or not in that case, whilst we are still unsure of the exact trial date, that the issues that Your Honour raised actually turn out to be the most important, as to whether or not in the circumstances, if Your Honour is not going to be the Presiding Judge - and I understand may not even be -- the Trial Chamber composition hasn't even been determined yet, so Your Honour may not be a Judge in any event at any part of the proceedings - it would be then a pity to take away the impact of hearing direct oral testimony, assuming that there's no advanced deterioration in the state of health. As I understand it, what we have at the moment is an assessment of the state of health of the witnesses based upon what they say, the witnesses themselves say, and their age, which is obviously not contested. There is no medical evidence, as I understand it, as such, beyond that. I'm not suggesting that there's anything less than -- the suggestions as to the health are anything less than accurate, but if it became an issue for the Trial Judge, the Presiding Judge, he may want, of course, medical evidence to support the contention. I don't know. I won't be asking for it because plainly it's not a question for me to make the decision, it's a question for the Judge to make a decision. I am content that if there is any real doubt as to the ability of these witnesses to attend because of their frailty, that in those circumstances depositions should be taken. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think -- I thank you, Mr. Morrison. I think I can decide this here and now orally, Mr. Von Hebel, and my decision is as follows: It is indicated that more or less the date when this trial will commence will be proximate to the date when the Prosecution intended to present these witnesses for the -- for the purposes of the motion filed by them on the 28th of February, 2003. There is no apparent reason given the circumstances surrounding the request of the Prosecution for the taking of depositions of these witnesses before the trial commences. In addition to the fact that this trial -- that this Pre-Trial Chamber thinks it is important not to deprive, as much as possible, the Trial Chamber that will try the accused in due course from the opportunity of hearing the evidence of these persons viva voce in the course of the trial. Because of this, or in view of this, the Trial Chamber decides not to grant the motion for the time being but reserves the right for the Prosecution to represent the motion as far as any of the six Prosecution witnesses that have been mentioned are concerned at any time should their state of health deteriorate or present a more serious reason for concern for the Prosecution. And in addition, the Pre-Trial Chamber reserves its position and also to provide differently should the dates when Trial Chamber -- when the trial will commence be further than early or mid-May, as envisaged now. So that's as far as pending motions are concerned. Disclosure. I know that this was also discussed during the 65 ter meeting, but I want to make sure that we are perfectly in order. I am informed, Mr. Yapa, that you would be in a position to complete Rule 66 disclosure by mid-May, and that you, Mr. Morrison, agree more or less with this deadline. I see you both nodding, so I have confirmation of this. Is there anything else either of you would like to add with regard to Rule 66 disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to what was required, we have -- we did mention to the senior legal officer at the 65 ter conference, made reference to the fact that in terms of Rule of 66(A)(i), all indictment supporting material have been disclosed, including the translations. In terms of Rule 66(A)(ii), there is one statement, it may be a 92 bis statement, which the Prosecution intends to disclose to the Defence, and it will be done in the very, very near future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I take it that Mr. Morrison has nothing to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Morrison. As regards Rule 68, I think I just need to remind both of you that there is -- that the obligation of the Prosecution is a continuing one, and I'm reminding you of this, Mr. Yapa, in particular, because in the previous Status Conference, you hinted that there may be some further need to -- for disclosure in this context at some future point in time. And since we're talking of November and now we are in March, I should like to know whether the position is still as you maintained it to be in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have been informed by the Senior Legal Officer of the position in respect of Rule 68 material. I can say with confidence at the moment that we have disclosed whatever that has been revealed to us, likely to be Rule 68 exculpatory material we have disclosed, and we have also been in contact with the Defence in respect of anything further that has to be done. We have asked the Defence as to whether they have any indication as to any other searches that we should do. So that also has been attended to. So I can say that up-to-date, whatever that has been disclosed, whatever that has been revealed to us as exculpatory material has been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, Mr. Morrison?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Next point on the agenda was agreed facts, but I am told that this more or less was dealt with exhaustively during the 65 ter meeting, and unless you indicate to me the contrary, I will not discuss this matter in this Status Conference. Protective measures, and obviously this is a very important matter. You will recall that we discussed this at the last Status Conference, and between that Status Conference and today, we handed -- Trial Chamber II handed down a decision which more or less covers -- a blanket provision for protective measures at this pre-trial stage. I need hardly indicate to you that when we have a date set for the beginning of the trial, for the trial, the situation needs to be addressed in a different fashion, and Mr. Yapa, the Prosecution will be required to file a fresh motion, as has been the practice so far in other cases, and which will address the protective measures required for each and every one of your witnesses when requested and where applicable but as they relate to their giving evidence in the trial. So we will require from you later on a comprehensive protective measures motion at the adequate -- at the right moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I also wanted to inform you or confirm to you that I as Pre-Trial Judge have been handed recently these last few days an updated, corrected version of the witnesses, list of witnesses that the Prosecution intends bringing forward in the course of the trial and that I have taken note of its contents. Trial date and timetable of pre-trial preparations. Obviously there is no point in starting this trial before the Appeals Chamber has decided -- have decided the interlocutory appeal on the jurisdiction and the legal arrest matter. As I said earlier, that is the decision of the Appeals Chamber, as far as we have been given to understand, is expected before mid-April, and that should pave the way either for the trial to start or for the proceedings to be dropped if the entire request of the Defence in the plea, preliminary plea, are upheld by the Appeals Chamber. So that means to say that the trial date depends almost entirely on the decision by the Appeals Chamber. But there is another caveat which is important: There is no point in my stating to you that the trial will start immediately after the decision by the Appeals Chamber. When I say "immediately," that means after providing each one of you, particularly the Defence, with enough time to come forward and start with the trial unless we have the certainty of having a Trial Chamber at our disposal. I'm saying this because, as you know, there are six trials going on at the moment which occupy fully the -- all the Judges, all the Judges that form part of this Tribunal, and there needs to be three Judges or at least one permanent Judge, one permanent Judge available in order to start this trial. It is my belief that that is also possible towards May, from -- starting from end of April. I state this subject to correction, of course, because what -- anything could happen and any one of the cases that are expected to finish more or less around about that time may take longer. But I can assure you, Mr. Morrison, that this particular case, also because of the time that your client has already spent in detention, is being given the utmost attention and top priority. If the Appeals Chamber decides against your client, Mr. Morrison, and once a date for the commencement of the trial is fixed, then obviously the Pre-Trial Judge, whoever that may be, will convene a Pre-Trial Conference as required by our Rules, usually a few days, a short time before the start of the trial. From previous experience, I can tell you that these pre-trial -- such a Pre-Trial Conference can be a very short one or can take quite some time, depending on the matters that need to be thrashed, but I don't see now in this particular case a Pre-Trial Conference can take place. Everything is indicative of quite a short and incisive Pre-Trial Conference. I also should like to inform you that once we all know when the case is going to start, when the trial is going to start, the senior legal officer of the Trial Chamber that will be dealing with the trial, that would be conducting the trial, will convene another 65 ter meeting to discuss any outstanding issues that there may be, and in particular, in particular, thrash out the protective measures matters. And for that purpose, it will be -- it is imperative that you are prepared, Mr. Yapa, to be in a position to file the comprehensive motion on protective measures in good time before this 65 ter meeting. I take it also that in the course of the 65 ter meeting that you had with our Senior Legal Officer, Mr. Von Hebel, you discussed also the anticipated length of the Prosecution's -- of the case for the Prosecution and the Defence case. I am told that more or less the case for the Prosecution is expected to last five full court weeks, but this means three witnesses being dropped from the original 40, list of 40, and depositions being taken, which would also mean that if depositions are not taken or if there is an increase in the number of witnesses, then you would require more than five weeks, but as I take it, we are still within this six to seven-week time frame. Do you agree with that estimate, Mr. Yapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. As far as the Defence case is concerned, I am informed that according to you, Mr. Morrison, at this present moment you find it difficult to give an estimate but are prepared to give a rough estimate of approximately one full working month. Do I take it that this is your idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be the absolute maximum. It's -- it's conceivable that if the Prosecution case takes five full working weeks, that any trial of the indictment as it now is could be concluded within two full working months, i.e., eight or thereabouts working weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Morrison. The next item on the agenda is assessment of Prosecution's case. I note that this also was discussed during the 65 ter meeting. I think it is important enough to merit some further comments on my part. I take it that you agree that in order to be in a position, both as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned and as far as the Defence is concerned, to make an assessment on the case of the Prosecution. When I say an assessment, I mean a real in-depth assessment, and in order to put the Trial Chamber, in particular, and also the Defence in a position to effectively prepare for the trial, it would be useful to have what we have referred to earlier as the proofing charts. Such charts are conceived under Rule 65 ter (E)(i) and (ii), the idea being to give an outline of evidence for each count on the basis of the summary of the witness's testimony and indicating for each witness the way the witness proposed would fit in the outline of evidence, the way suggested exhibits may fit in with the outline of evidence, and the way facts which you may agree upon between you before the trial may fit in within the outline, the parameters of the evidence. I know that you have been shown a sort of a sample or an example of an exhaustive document, exhaustive exercise along these lines coming from another case, and I also know that more or less, Mr. Yapa, the Prosecution indicated that they should or they anticipate that they would be in a position to provide the Trial Chamber with these charts before mid-April. I want a confirmation of that because that is absolutely important if the trial itself is expected to start sometime in mid-May or late May.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour, for the opportunity given. In fact, this is one of the matters I wanted to take up. After Your Honour's explanation as to the purpose of the proofing chart, I don't think I have to raise that question, because at the stage when the senior legal officer mentioned this at the 65 ter conference, although I thought that I had a general idea as to what was required, I thought there were certain matters that needed to be clarified. But those matters have been clarified by Your Honour. So I must say at the outset that we are willing and prepared to do that exercise and to submit proofing charts by the date indicated, by mid-April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It should be -- it shouldn't be a difficult exercise at all because we are talking here of a relatively small number of witnesses. I thank you. Do you need to comment on this, Mr. Morrison, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, save to endorse that it is a good idea. I prosecute in England quite a lot, and it's something that we always -- in the last four or five years it's been the practice of the Crown to produce such a chart. It also, of course, in the English system it helps the Judge summing up to the jury. It's not an issue in this Tribunal, although I should imagine the same exercise can be undertaken with a view to forming a judgement. So I think it's a very helpful exercise all round.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Morrison. Indeed, I fully agree with you that it is a very important exercise. We are coming to the end. Are there any procedural matters, issues that either of you would like to raise at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: With Your Honour's permission, I'm convinced that Your Honour may have been informed of the -- what transpired at the 65 ter meeting, every matter. There was one matter that I raised in terms of Rule 67 of the Rules and regulations -- Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal. My learned friend very clearly stated as to what his position is, but I'm making reference to that at this stage because this is a requirement in terms of Rule 67 for the Defence whenever defence of alibi or a defence of like nature is taken up. So it is for that purpose. We have not been provided with anything yet, but my learned friend said that -- it refers only to a few counts, not all the counts, but my learned friend made it clear that beyond what was stated at the interview with the accused, there was nothing more to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour will appreciate the difficulty. The Defence position, which is quite plain from the interviews given by the defendant in this case, is that he was not present at the time when a number of the incidents alleged to have happened took place. In a lot of cases, the dates are not given with any particularity, or the times are not given with any particularity. It is known that the defendant was present at the camp when it was his time to be there according to a duty roster. When he was not at the camp, the position is plain that he was back in the town at Vlasenica, living a normal domestic existence. But without the opportunity to be given exact dates or exact times, and especially after the amount of time that has passed, it is simply possible for the defendant to give any meaningful alibi in the sense of producing a witness who will say, "Oh, yes. At that particular time on that particular day I was -" for instance - "having a cup of coffee with the defendant at a cafe in Vlasenica, therefore he couldn't have been at the camp." That sort of evidence simply isn't available to the Defence and it will never be available in circumstances where the indictment is necessarily vague as to exact timings and where the opportunity for giving alibi evidence is simply to say, "I wasn't present. I don't know whether what was alleged to have happened did happen, but in any event, I wasn't present either at the scene or necessarily at the camp." And I don't think he's going to be able to go beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What you say is indeed very reasonable, Mr. Morrison, but what about those events for which there is a specific date indicated?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, where it is possible to do so in a way that is going to assist the Court, I will undertake that we will endeavour to produce a notice of alibi, but I forewarn everyone that it is likely to be in vague rather than precise terms because of the passage of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in any case, there is the ultimate solution of crossing swords with any witness during your cross-examination and taking issue when there is something that you obviously want to contest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So more or less there. But Prosecution does have a right to be -- to have advance notification on any alibi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the object of giving alibi notice is to prevent the Defence from ambushing the Prosecution at trial with an alibi that wasn't previously indicated. All I can say is that there will be no such ambush and no such attempt at ambush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Does that satisfy you, Mr. Yapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any other procedural matter or issue you would like to raise? It's taken that there is no further procedural matter that you would like to raise. Mr. Nikolic, should -- should you like to raise any matter relating to the -- your detention in the Detention Unit and to your state of health, mental or physical, that you think ought to be brought to the notice of this Trial Chamber -- or Pre-Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I said last time, the only thing is that I've been here quite a long time. Otherwise, I don't have any other problems. I feel healthy. I have become accustomed to this way of life, if I can put it that way, and I don't think I have anything of any substance to add and present to you here. My lawyers have already stated what I wanted them to say. The conditions in the Detention Unit are quite normal, especially in the building we've been put up now. The greatest problem is the length of the proceedings themselves. The indictment was raised in 1994 against me, so that's quite a long time ago. And that is the only thing I have to say and my only remarks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Morrison, is there anything else that you should like to point out in relation to these matters, these issues, his state of health and his condition of detention? Is there anything that is of concern to you except for the length of time that has been taken before this trial starts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. It's -- it's plainly the longer the person is in custody and the greater the length of time between the events in issue and the trial, the worse everybody's memory becomes. So that's the only issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Prosecution is trying to solve that by taking depositions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: That's why I don't object in principle to depositions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Morrison. And is there anything else either of you would like to mention, raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Nothing from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I thank you both, and the Status Conference stands adjourned.
